title: Dove Creek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dove Creek wells have a 152 ft median depth; see expected yield, water levels, permit history, risks and drilling costs.
h1: Dove Creek Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Dove Creek means looking closely at the well record, not just the listing. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a typical depth of 152 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock can produce very different results from one lot to the next. The records also show a median reported yield of 5.0 gallons per minute, although only 9 wells report a pump yield.

This guide covers the local drilling range, water levels, permit history, likely construction cost and the checks that matter before you buy or build in Dove Creek, Lewis, Dolores, Cortez or the surrounding Dolores County area.

sections.heading: Dove Creek well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Among the 79 constructed wells that report total depth, the median is 152 feet. The middle half runs from 120 to 215 feet, which is a useful range for early budgeting but not a guarantee for a particular parcel. A driller's bid should allow for local variation in the bedrock.

Most recorded wells, 73%, are between 100 and 300 feet. Another 19% are under 100 feet, while 6% fall between 300 and 600 feet and 1% reach beyond 600 feet. The deepest record is 640 feet. Permits identify the local water source mainly as unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with a small number naming the Dakota aquifer or Dakota Group Aquifer.

sections.heading: What a Dove Creek well may produce
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 5.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of reported results is 4.5 to 13.0 gallons per minute. The mix is broad: 11% of wells report under 1 gallon per minute, 22% report 1 to 5, 44% report 5 to 15, and 22% report more than 15.

Only 9 permitted wells report a pump yield, so these figures are a guide rather than a complete survey of every well. A low-producing well may still work for a household with adequate storage, but the buyer should ask how the yield was tested, how long the test ran and what the well is legally permitted to serve. Household-use exempt wells remain subject to their permit conditions.

sections.heading: Dove Creek water levels and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 4 wells report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is limited. Within that small record set, the median depth to water is 95 feet, with the middle half from 72 to 122 feet. That is useful for planning pump setting and trench work, but it should not be treated as a complete groundwater map.

The permit counts by decade do not establish a water-table trend. They show activity rather than repeated water-level measurements: 4 permits in the 1960s, 17 in the 1970s, 19 in the 1980s, 8 in the 1990s, 13 in the 2000s, 6 in the 2010s and 5 in the 2020s. A parcel-specific water-level check is more meaningful than assuming the table is rising or falling across Dove Creek.

sections.heading: Who drilled near Dove Creek and when permits were issued
sections.html:
Dove Creek's permit history is spread across several decades, with the newest permit in 2024. The records include 110 wells, of which 79 are recorded as constructed. That difference matters: a permit map is not the same as a map of completed, working wells, and buyers should review the actual construction and pump information for nearby parcels.

The most active drillers in the records are Kilby'S Water Well Service, also listed as Kilby, Edward E, with 12 wells; Fritz Erickson Mining, also listed as Erickson, Richard, with 8; and Mcpherson Drilling Co., also listed as Mcpherson, Billy G., with 8. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or a current quote. Confirm licensing, availability and scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Dove Creek well drilling cost in fractured bedrock
sections.html:
The cost model for Dove Creek assumes fractured mountain bedrock such as granite or gneiss. At the 152-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $9,900 to $15,200, based on a rate of $65 to $100 per foot. The finished well estimate is $15,900 to $27,200 after adding a pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work.

Those figures are tied to the median depth, not a guaranteed bid. A 300-foot or deeper hole can move the budget substantially, while access, casing, grout, water testing, power distance, storage requirements and difficult drilling conditions can also change the total. Ask for a written estimate that separates drilling from completion and clearly states what happens if the hole is dry or produces too little water.

sections.heading: Dove Creek risks to check before building
sections.html:
Yield is the first practical risk. Eleven percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, and fractured rock can change quickly across short distances. The permit data also include 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 4 historic mine features within about 10 miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped area, but that does not replace testing the well serving the property.

Check the well permit, construction report, pump test and recent water-quality results. Review casing and grout details, then locate the septic system and reserve area before finalizing a house site. Septic setbacks, access for a drill rig, electrical service and a dependable year-round driveway can be as important as the estimated hole depth. Ask Colorado DWR about permit limits, and confirm whether an augmentation plan is needed in the applicable basin.

sections.heading: A sensible plan for a Dove Creek lot
sections.html:
Before closing, compare the subject parcel with nearby permitted wells and focus on wells that are actually constructed and report depth, yield or water level. The records around Lewis, Dolores, Cortez, Naturita, Redvale and Towaoc can provide broader regional context, but conditions at the lot still control the decision.

For a new build, obtain a site-specific drilling proposal, confirm the intended domestic or household use, and budget for the complete system rather than the drilled hole alone. Have the water tested before relying on it, and make sure the septic layout, driveway and building envelope work together. If the proposed well is weak, storage may help, but it does not solve every permit, water-quality or long-term reliability problem.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dove Creek, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Dove Creek is 152 feet. The middle half of wells is 120 to 215 feet, but the records range from under 100 feet to a deepest recorded well of 640 feet. Most wells, 73%, are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the exact depth parcel-specific.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dove Creek?
faq.a: At the local median depth of 152 feet, drilling alone is estimated at $9,900 to $15,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical work is estimated at $15,900 to $27,200. The final bid can change with depth, access, casing, grout, power distance, storage needs and difficult fractured-bedrock conditions.

faq.q: How much water does a Dove Creek well produce?
faq.a: Reported well yields have a 5.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 4.5 to 13.0 gallons per minute. The records are limited because only 9 wells report a pump yield. Eleven percent report under 1 gallon per minute, so obtain a pump test and verify the permit before depending on a well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Dove Creek?
faq.a: The permit map identifies 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 4 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped facts do not determine a particular well's quality. Test the well serving the property for appropriate contaminants, especially before drinking it or moving into a new home.

faq.q: Are water levels falling near Dove Creek?
faq.a: The available records do not show a reliable falling or rising trend. Only 4 wells report static water levels. Among those, the median depth to water is 95 feet, with the middle half from 72 to 122 feet. Permit counts by decade describe drilling activity, not groundwater change, so check current conditions at the specific property.
